prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset: production sprite atlas for Cosmic: A Sea Beneath the Moon. Input image1 is a STYLE reference only: retain the medallion form, palette, grain and physical depiction approach, but create the NEW requested subjects below. Exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, 16 circles total. Regular equal square cells, Use a SQUARE canvas, exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, equal square cells, no outer margin. Aim2048px wide. Every circle diameter84%of its cell, centred, with generous fully transparent gutters; leave allcells complete and separated. No extra cells or objects. Original astronomical chromolithograph with dry-gouache and chalk masses: deep indigo circular fields, feathered warm-ivory light, amber heat, copper/charcoal minerals and restrained teal water. Simplify to broad meaningful structures visible at72px. Fine grain stays in subjects; generous quiet dark space. One thin ivory circular outline. No glossy UI buttons, photographic lens flare, ornamental decoration, humans, machines, text, labels, numerals, formulas or grid lines. Inside each circle the field is opaque; outside circles true alpha transparency. No shadows, rays or fragments beyond circles. Atom/particle diagrams are schematic: tiny compact ivory dots and diffuse electron-probability clouds, never planetary electron orbits; individual nuclei do NOT glow like stars. Exact invisible chemistry is communicated by game names/readings, never by invented diagnostic coloration. All terrestrial worlds have bare mineral terrain; no plants, life or modern continents. Early Moon is pale gray-ivory without familiar dark maria. All Earth cutaways are views of one continuing world.
Strict row-major subjects (left to right, then top to bottom):
1. Persistent heavy rain: A broad dark-bottomed pale cloud sends a dense curtain of long rain strokes across the medallion. Avoid: Dense continuous rain, no mountain or completed basin fill.
2. Rain remaining on the ground: Rain visibly ends as small teal wet patches on the cool basalt beside the separate amber lava channel. Avoid: Thin surviving surface water, not deep pools or an already filled sea.
3. Hollows in the volcanic rock: Two linked but dry shallow hollows in a rough dark basalt slab, an asymmetric notch at the near rim. Avoid: Keep this hollow geometry in water-filled states; no water or biological soil.
4. A slope toward a broad basin: A broad bare basalt slope descends diagonally from the right inland ridge toward the sheltered central basin. Avoid: Dry connected topography; no stream, sea or vegetation.
5. A less permeable layer: A cutaway of fractured dark rock above one continuous denser horizontal layer, no water yet. Avoid: Layered permeability contrast rather than a wall, pipe or impermeable manmade membrane.
6. Pools on the cooling rock: The established two shallow basalt hollows now hold small separate teal pools, rims still mostly dry. Avoid: Rain pools in the same rock; no marine waves or flooded tidal connection.
7. Runoff toward the basin: A thin branching teal ribbon travels down the established diagonal bare basalt slope toward a still mostly empty basin. Avoid: Connected shallow runoff, not an already large river or ocean.
8. An accumulating early sea: A broad teal surface occupies the sheltered basin between the established stepped left headland and lower right rocky ridge. Avoid: No dissolved-chemistry colour change, mature sand beach, tidal pools or organisms.
9. Water entering fractured rock: A basalt cutaway shows a thin teal route entering from the surface and descending through branching cracks. Avoid: Land rain infiltration, not seawater beneath an ocean.
10. Groundwater diverted sideways: The same descending fracture route turns sideways along the top of the dense horizontal rock layer. Avoid: Horizontal subsurface route; no invented pipe and no surface spring yet.
11. A spring above the shore: A short teal flow emerges from a side fracture halfway down the bare basalt slope, then falls toward lower ground. Avoid: Visible rock emergence point; no whole inlet or pre-existing river source.
12. A freshwater inlet: The spring's narrow teal channel meets the broad early sea at a bare rocky mouth, different flow directions shown softly. Avoid: Fresh versus saline water is not colour-coded; identify route, not invisible chemistry.
13. Carbon dioxide in the air: One enlarged linear three-centre molecule in a faint atmospheric wisp, pale diffuse bonded lobes without letters. Avoid: Schematic molecule, no coloured poison cloud or breathable-air emblem.
14. A sheltered patch of water: A small sheltered teal inlet behind a dark basalt shoulder, nearly smooth surface and no incoming wave crests. Avoid: Open connection to sea remains visible; not a closed rock pool.
15. Rain with dissolved carbon dioxide: A rain streak passes through a faint atmospheric molecular wisp and reaches a dark basalt edge. Avoid: Rain stays normal-looking water; no green acid, corrosive glow or instant melted coastline.
16. Basalt changing under water: A wet fractured basalt face with a shallow rough altered rind and a few loosened angular grains at its foot. Avoid: Subtle rock alteration, no soil, roots, moss or dramatic colour-coded chemistry.

Image2 is the APPROVED COAST GEOGRAPHY reference. For any shore or pool subject keep its stepped LEFT headland and low RIGHT ridge. Any hollows/pools are the same threebasins: LARGE foreground-right pool, smaller mid-left pool and small distant middle pool, same connecting basalt rims. Waterlevel orlighting maychange; rockgeometry andcamera mustnot. Water-chemistry detailviews may use closer crops of these materials. No invented bottles, vessels, observers or biological scenery.
